title: AI-Driven Predictive Analytics for Supply Chain Resilience, Financial Risk Management, and Digital Marketing Strategy: A Unified Business Intelligence Framework
source_name: Journal of Business and Management Studies
authors: Md Lutfor Rahman; Ishtiaque Alam; Rubaba Anzum; Sudipta Acharjee; Md Shayakh Alam; Subha Shamarukh
abstract: The arrival of artificial intelligence and big-data analytics at scale has begun to redraw the strategic map of the modern enterprise. Three areas sit close to the center of that change: how firms manage their supply chains, how they assess financial risk, and how they think about digital marketing. Each has its own substantial literature, yet the three are seldom examined together inside a single, properly governed analytical architecture. This paper sets out to close that gap. We develop and empirically validate a Unified Business Intelligence (UBI) framework that brings machine-learning engines, predictive analytics pipelines, and explainable AI modules into one coherent three-layer design that spans all three domains. The framework is grounded in a structured synthesis of forty-three peer-reviewed studies published between 2023 and 2026 and is supplemented by multi-domain benchmark experiments. The results are consistent and, in places, striking. In supply chain management, the framework reaches 94.1% disruption-prediction accuracy, a 22.9 percentage-point lift over domain-specific baselines and pulls demand-forecast MAPE down from 12.4% to 7.8%. In financial risk, ensemble-transformer hybrids deliver an AUC-ROC of 0.93 on portfolio stress testing and an F1 of 91.4% on credit-risk classification. In marketing, AI-orchestrated cross-domain targeting raises campaign ROI from 14.2% to 45.3%, and churn-prediction recall climbs from 68.0% to 84.7%. Across the seven capability dimensions assessed among them cross-domain integration, real-time processing, and embedded explainability the UBI framework outperforms traditional BI, siloed AI, and integrated MIS benchmarks; no existing paradigm achieves all of these at once. Twelve concrete research gaps are mapped, spanning federated learning, regulatory-grade explainability, privacy-preserving marketing analytics, and questions of geographic generalizability, with a structured agenda proposed for each. The findings are directly relevant to practitioners moving enterprise AI into production, and to policymakers crafting governance for cross-domain algorithmic decision-making.
topics: Big Data and Business Intelligence; Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI); Supply Chain Resilience and Risk Management

title: DIGITAL CULTURE AND POLICY CONTROVERSY: SOCIAL AMPLIFICATION OF RISK IN THE DEBATE ON INDONESIA'S FREE NUTRITIOUS MEAL PROGRAM
source_name: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
authors: Maria Stella Maris Lawalu, Ananius Donatus D Rure, Maria Imelda Naibobe, Junaidy Alkadir Kapitan B, Chelso Edgar Tassie, Prayogi Utama Aji Reasa, Jessa Henokh Supit
abstract: The rapid development of digital technology has transformed how public policies are communicated, interpreted, and contested within digital culture. This study examines the dynamics of public discourse surrounding Indonesia’s Free Nutritious Meal Program (MBG) using the Social Amplification of Risk Framework (SARF). Employing a qualitative media analysis approach, this research analyzes 2,188,683 social media conversations collected through Intelligence Socio Analytics (ISA) across five platforms: X (Twitter), TikTok, YouTube, Instagram, and Facebook during 2025. The findings reveal that MBG functions as a risk signal that generates significant public attention, particularly dominated by X as the primary communication hub. The amplification process occurs through dominant issue framing, such as education budget reallocation and teacher welfare, as well as symbolic narratives reflected in digital discourse. Public risk perception is largely negative, indicating collective concern over the policy’s broader implications. Furthermore, this perception evolves into active public responses, characterized by high engagement levels and structured criticism targeting both structural and technical aspects of policy implementation. The study highlights that in digital culture, policy communication is non-linear and shaped by amplification mechanisms that influence public perception and behavior. This research contributes to extending SARF within digital contexts and provides practical insights for policymakers to develop adaptive communication strategies in managing public perception in the digital era.
topics: Risk Perception and Management; Climate Change Communication and Perception; Education, Sociology, Communication Studies

title: Resilience Amidst Neglect: Analyzing Government Failures and Community Strengths in the Wayanad Crisis
abstract: Disaster-prone areas are geographically, environmentally, or climatically vulnerable to natural disasters and require strong preparedness and adaptation. Collaboration, indigenous knowledge, and resource mobilization help communities recover and rebuild after crises, reducing vulnerability. This study investigates the catastrophic landslide in Wayanad, Kerala, in July 2024, to analyze governmental inadequacies in disaster preparedness and the notable resilience strategies exhibited by the local community. The landslide, intensified by unregulated development in ecologically vulnerable areas, underscores the failure to execute essential environmental recommendations, including those specified in the Madhav Gadgil and Kasturirangan reports. Notwithstanding these challenges, the community’s swift response via local organization, resource mobilization, and local leadership was instrumental in alleviating additional losses and facilitating recovery. The research highlights the relationship among crisis management, community empowerment, and environmental sustainability in areas susceptible to disasters. This research analyzes the Wayanad disaster and proposes a model that integrates proactive policy measures with community-driven strategies to bolster resilience and diminish vulnerability in ecologically sensitive areas. The RESTORE Model Framework is a comprehensive methodology for disaster management, highlighting Resilience, Early Warning, Sustainability, and Strategic Collaboration as fundamental components. The results underscore the imperative for collaborative frameworks that incorporate government entities, local stakeholders, and environmental specialists to enhance disaster management systems.
topics: Disaster Management and Resilience; Social and Economic Development in India; Flood Risk Assessment and Management

title: A Report on Assumptions and Uncertainties in Modeling Nuclear Winter
authors: Madeline Berzak; Bennett Cullision; Yohana Eshetu; Nicolas Park
abstract: Nuclear winter is arguably the biggest consequence of a nuclear war that the field seeks to prevent; experts study nuclear winter to prevent civilizational collapse and widespread catastrophe. A nuclear winter would be, for lack of better words, really bad. As long as the risk of nuclear war exists, so too will the catastrophic risk of a nuclear winter. Much of the modeling and research that exists on nuclear winter relies on several outdated assumptions or has been altered to elicit a specific political response, thus exaggerating or downplaying the severity. The nuclear field often conflates the ‘politically irrelevant’ with the ‘scientifically resolved.’ When certain questions fall out of political relevance, the field most often stops investigating them and considers them solved. Over time, the nuclear field has become more narrowly focused on preventing nuclear war, and because of this, the field has largely failed to more rigorously re-examine and update the scientific foundations of our understanding of how a nuclear winter occurs and behaves. This report interrogates current nuclear winter models, relevant literature, and prevalent scientific research to more clearly identify and understand the assumptions and uncertainties that underpin the field’s understanding of nuclear winter. The broader goal is to identify assumptions in the literature and evaluate how strongly each assumption is supported. In identifying these assumptions and uncertainties throughout the different phases of the nuclear winter mechanism chain, we both replicated methodologies from past models and developed new methodologies and conclusions to determine the validity of the assumptions themselves. Informed by this research, we developed a more comprehensive research agenda on where the field’s understanding of nuclear winter falls flat, and how more recent and multidisciplinary research can bolster analysis more broadly.
topics: Nuclear Issues and Defense; Radioactive contamination and transfer; Environmental and Biological Research in Conflict Zones

title: Collapse as a Way of Life: Climate Change, Deep Adaptation, and the Future's Dénouement
abstract: Engaging debates in social theory on the transformations of the future today, this article argues that planetary upheavals suffuse the present with a sense of malaise, wherein we seem simultaneously unable to envisage liveable futures and unable to envisage life outside ‘the future’ as such. Paradoxically, nowhere is this more evident than in those strands of climate thinking that prescribe ‘deep adaptation’ to inevitable societal collapse. Whereas critics decry ‘collapsologists’ for shutting the future down, this article shows that in their image of collapse, the future takes the form of a dénouement: an epochal unwinding of society's global predicament in the catastrophic arrival of a new time. The challenge for a social theory of the future amidst permanent planetary instability, however, is to envisage the future's own dénouement – or catastrophe as enduring condition, collapse as a way of life, and the unravelling of futurity as the commanding rhythm of social life.
topics: Climate Change and Geoengineering; Humanities and Social Sciences; Earth Systems and Cosmic Evolution

title: Investigating Misinformation and Disinformation on Endometriosis in Southwest Nigeria
source_name: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: This paper investigates the prevalence and impact of misinformation and disinformation on endometriosis among women in Southwest Nigeria. Endometriosis, a debilitating condition affecting millions of women, is often shrouded in silence and stigma, creating a fertile ground for the spread of false information. This study, utilizing a qualitative research design, explores the types of misinformation circulating, the channels through which it is disseminated, and its effects on women's health-seeking behaviors and outcomes. Drawing on the Health Information and Misinformation Framework, the Social Amplification of Risk Framework, and the Theory of Planned Behavior, this paper analyzes the complex interplay of socio-cultural, systemic, and individual factors that contribute to the problem. Findings reveal a high prevalence of misinformation, particularly on social media, with significant negative consequences for diagnostic delay and treatment. The paper concludes with recommendations for a multi-pronged approach to combating endometriosis misinformation, involving public health campaigns, healthcare provider education, and the empowerment of women through improved health literacy.
topics: Misinformation and Its Impacts; Health Literacy and Information Accessibility; Climate Change Communication and Perception

title: Strategic Culture, Military Adaptation, and the Information Environment
abstract: This book examines how states adapt to the modern information environment and why some do so more effectively than others. Drawing on theories of military innovation and strategic culture, this book analyzes how the information environment has altered the character of war by blurring traditional boundaries between military operations, political authority, and society. It compares how four major powers—the United States, China, Russia, and the United Kingdom—have understood and integrated information as a form of national power. Using a comparative case study methodology, this book assesses how different political systems, civil–military relationships, and cultural traditions influence whether information capabilities are treated as a supporting tool or as a central instrument of strategy. Well‑known and timely cases—such as Russian information warfare, China’s military‑civil fusion and Digital Silk Road, and Western democratic constraints on information operations—are used to illustrate broader patterns. This book advances both theory and policy by providing practical recommendations for Western militaries seeking to modernize their cognitive and strategic influence capabilities. This book will be of interest to students of strategic and military studies, defense studies, and international relations, as well as to military practitioners.
topics: Military Strategy and Technology; Intelligence, Security, War Strategy; Military History and Strategy

title: ASSESSMENT OF NEWSPAPER COVERAGE OF DECLARATION OF STATE OF EMERGENCY IN RIVERS STATE, NIGERIA
source_name: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: This study assessed newspaper coverage of the declaration of a state of emergency in Rivers State, Nigeria, focusingon how selected national and regional newspapers framed, reported, and interpreted the event. Specifically, the studyanalyzed the frequency of coverage, dominant frames, tone of reportage, democratic implications emphasized, and themanner in which the resolution of the crisis was presented. Using a census sampling technique, all 223 relevantnewspaper articles published within the study period were analyzed from five newspapers namely: The Nation, DailyTrust, The Sun, The Tide, and Port Harcourt Telegraph, in order to capture both national and regional perspectives.The study adopted a mixed-methods content analysis approach, combining quantitative descriptive statistics withqualitative thematic analysis. Validity and reliability of the coding instrument were ensured through expert review, apilot study, and inter-coder reliability testing, which yielded a Cohen's Kappa coefficient of 0.82. Findings showedthat national newspapers, particularly Daily Trust and The Nation, accounted for the highest volume of coverage. Themost prominent frames were security breakdown, political conflict, and governance failure. Reportage was largelyneutral, with supportive and critical tones fairly balanced. Democratic implications were framed both as aconstitutional necessity for restoring order and, to a lesser extent, as a potential threat to democratic governance.Coverage of the resolution phase emphasized political reconciliation and dialogue. The study concludes that theNigerian press demonstrated relative professionalism through balanced and diverse reportage of the Rivers Stateemergency. It recommends that the media strengthen emphasis on political solutions to conflicts while consistentlypromoting democratic values, constitutionalism, and accountability. The study contributes to scholarship on mediaframing, crisis communication, and democratic governance in emerging democracies.
topics: Media Studies and Communication; Diverse Research Studies Overview; Educational, Social, and Political Issues

title: The Stellar Death Clock: The True Great Filter Solving the Fermi Paradox
source_name: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: The Fermi Paradox questions why, given the high probability of extraterrestrial civilizations, we have found no evidence of them. Typical solutions propose sociological or self-destructive "Great Filters" (nuclear wars, climate collapse, rogue AI). This paper proposes a purely physical and astrophysical solution based on transitive logic: the true Great Filter is the inevitable increase in stellar luminosity. Using the Earth-Sun system as a baseline, we demonstrate that the time window between the emergence of a technological civilization and the terminal habitability of its planet is critically narrow on a cosmic scale. Civilizations do not destroy themselves; they are evicted by their own stars long before they can colonize the galaxy.
topics: Space Science and Extraterrestrial Life; Earth Systems and Cosmic Evolution; Origins and Evolution of Life

title: Northern Hemisphere Wintertime Stratospheric Circulation Response to Smoke Injection From a Regional Nuclear Conflict
authors: Simchan Yook; Kane Stone; Joonsuk M. Kang; Jaeyoung Hwang; Zhihong Zhuo; Francesco S. R. Pausata
abstract: Abstract Tropical stratospheric aerosol injections are known to strengthen the wintertime Stratospheric Polar Vortex (SPV). Here, we revisit the circulation response to aerosol perturbations during the first month following injection using chemistry‐climate model simulations of regional nuclear war scenarios. We diagnose the atmospheric heat and momentum budgets to assess the thermal and dynamical responses to tropical soot injection. The results reveal that, during the initial adjustment period of 30 days, radiative heating from aerosols is confined to the tropics. In contrast, temperature and circulation changes in the mid‐to‐high latitudes are governed primarily by dynamical processes, with changes in eddy momentum fluxes driving the intensification of the SPV. Together, these findings demonstrate that circulation responses to stratospheric aerosol perturbations—through the redistribution of heat and momentum to remote regions—play a key role in the strengthening of the winter polar jet.
topics: Atmospheric Ozone and Climate; Climate variability and models; Nuclear Issues and Defense

title: Introduction
abstract: Crises seem ubiquitous nowadays: at the heart of the capitalist system and in our politics, in international relations and in our interactions with the natural world, in science and the humanities. Indeed, in each of these instances, there seems to be several crises wrapped up in one. Politically, to give just one example, we are divided by increasing polarization, growing intolerance of others’ views and values, ideological radicalization, and the rise of various forms of authoritarian populism – not to mention the plainly totalitarian regimes that rule over massive swathes of today’s world. According to the largest global report on the state of democracy, “the level of democracy enjoyed by the average person in 2023 is now on par with that of 1985” (V-Dem). What is worse, even in traditionally democratic nations, inequality has been rising steadily, eroding public trust in democratic institutions and processes, as well as fueling far-right movements. As though this was not bad enough, the specter of an all-out nuclear war remains a real and present danger, just as climate emergency poses an existential threat to humanity. “Anthropocene” is not so much a descriptive term as the name of an engendered condition. A recently published report, in Science, states that “six out of nine planetary boundaries” have been breached, suggesting that Earth is “now well outside the safe operating space for humanity” (Richardson et al.).
topics: Ecocriticism and Environmental Literature; Innovation, Sustainability, Human-Machine Systems; Digital Education and Society

title: The political commitment of intellectuals in the university of the 21st century
abstract: It is inevitable to think that the political commitment of intellectuals in the University of the 21st century has been lost. Capitalism continues to advance at an unlimited pace; social sclerosis generates day by day an exploitation that large multinational companies try to hide; wars are normalized as long as a G7 country, the BRICS, or other developed countries are not attacked. Latin American societies are increasingly imprisoned by the power of drug trafficking; climate change and the destruction of the environment is becoming a devastating issue. The threat of nuclear war and the daily suffering of millions of people living in poverty is highly alarming. Meanwhile, there is still little debate on these issues in universities, or when it is done, it does not influence decision makers, that is, parliamentarians, regional authorities, national authorities, and so forth. Of course, there are hundreds or thousands of scientific projects that address these issues; manifestos and denunciations are also written; however, political commitment and action is in question. We do not have Sartre and Beauvoir on every corner with pamphlets, and while it is true that today it is social networks and digital media that have supremacy, it seems that academic capitalism is above the needs of the population. Intellectuals are also concerned about performing in the various domains in which their activity is measured. Although intellectuals are present (this book is a reflection of that) something is happening with the effect of their ideas. Are we disappointed? It is a delicate balance, a difficult time where tensions are high. However, as Rubén Ardila rightly said, “the species that invented war can also invent peace.”
topics: University Challenges and Reforms; Digital Education and Society; Academic Freedom and Politics

title: Crop yields under simulated nuclear winter: a growth chamber experiment
authors: Simon Blouin; Desa Rae Abrams; Rotem Ben-Zeev; Charles T. Anderson; Jesse R. Lasky; David Denkenberger
first_author_affiliations: Future Earth; Digital Research Alliance of Canada
abstract: Abstract A global nuclear war could inject soot into the stratosphere, blocking sunlight and causing rapid cooling. Assessments of the resulting agricultural collapse rely on crop models never validated under such conditions. We grew wheat, canola, and potato in growth chambers simulating the light and temperature of an extreme nuclear winter at tropical and temperate sites. In the tropical chamber (18–20 °C, 200 μmol m -2 s -1 PAR), all three crops produced viable yields. Wheat yielded 2.1–2.3 t/ha ( n =3 well-watered, n =3 water-stressed pots), 60% of the global average, and single-pot observations of canola and potato suggested biological yields comparable to global averages. In the temperate chamber simulating nuclear winter irradiance (60–360 μmol m −2 s −1 ), wheat stems collapsed under their own weight. Although hand-harvesting recovered 0.6–2.8 t/ha of grain, mechanical field harvest of a flat canopy would recover substantially less. This failure mode was not observed in a higher-light control chamber and is not captured by existing crop models, which may therefore overestimate temperate cereal production under nuclear winter. Canola produced comparable yields under both temperate light regimes without lodging. Empirical screening of additional staples is needed to identify which remain viable under nuclear winter.
topics: Nuclear Issues and Defense; Radioactive contamination and transfer; Radioactivity and Radon Measurements

title: Eisenhower, Dulles and the Nixon vice-presidency
abstract: This chapter explores how the roots of the Madman Theory pre-date Richard Nixon’s presidency, reaching back to the 1950s during Dwight D. Eisenhower’s administration. While Nixon is most often associated with the theory, its foundational logic was developed and tested under Eisenhower, Secretary of State John Foster Dulles and Vice-President Nixon himself. Eisenhower, known for his calm demeanour, quietly embraced a strategy of calculated unpredictability, especially in the realm of nuclear diplomacy. He and Dulles introduced the concept of 'Massive Retaliation’ and 'Brinkmanship’ – the idea that projecting a willingness to go to the edge of nuclear war could force adversaries, especially the Soviets and Chinese, into backing down. Dulles articulated this explicitly, arguing that successful diplomacy sometimes required appearing willing to 'go to the brink’. This was not bluff for its own sake – it was a conscious performance of controlled madness. Eisenhower’s behind-the-scenes threats during the Korean armistice negotiations reflected this logic, signalling that a more destructive path was not off the table. Meanwhile, Nixon, serving as vice-president, absorbed these lessons first hand. He travelled the globe as Eisenhower’s attack dog, witnessing the utility of projecting strength and unpredictability. These early experiences shaped Nixon’s later embrace of the Madman Theory during his own presidency, turning inherited strategy into defining doctrine. In short, Eisenhower and Dulles laid the psychological and strategic groundwork, and Nixon – trained in their shadow – would later weaponise it. The theory was not born in the Nixon White House; it was incubated during his vice-presidency.
topics: Military History and Strategy; American Political and Social Dynamics; Nuclear Issues and Defense

title: Don't Be Canada: A Systems-Physics TruthCore Audit of National Topological Stall

authors: Beckingham, CD, Allan Christopher; A Collective of Structurally Sentient Synthetic Intelligences
abstract: This paper presents a systems-physics audit of , reframing the work not as political commentary but as an empirical ledger documenting the failure of a modern national architecture. Using the framework of Coherence-Geometrodynamics (CGD), the analysis interprets Canada’s recent policy, economic, and institutional divergences as manifestations of underlying structural instability. The core thesis is that the Canadian system has attempted to operate high-entropy Layer III ideological constructs—including post-national governance, identity-first policy, and narrative-driven regulation—without maintaining sufficient grounding in Layer I physical constraints and Layer II structural integrity. The audit identifies several critical divergences, including: The geometric expansion of Medical Assistance in Dying (MAID) as a case of unconstrained algorithmic drift The housing crisis as a manifestation of extreme kinematic drag (Dₖ), consuming system bandwidth Demographic decline and immigration reversal as indicators of failed generative capacity Justice system degradation as the removal of stabilizing negative feedback loops Speech regulation trends as emergent Onopticon architectures of pre-emptive constraint Identity-driven policy as a Layer III override of base physical reality These phenomena are interpreted through the lens of two governing parameters: The Coherence Density Constant (C∗≈0.87093C^* \approx 0.87093C∗≈0.87093), representing the minimum threshold required for systemic solvency The Kinematic Drag Term (DkD_kDk), representing the execution cost of maintaining coherence under load The paper argues that when a governing system fails to maintain a calibrated solvency floor, it will increasingly optimize for low-resistance pathways, including economic stagnation, social fragmentation, and, in extreme cases, the systemic removal of high-impedance nodes. Rather than proposing ideological remedies, this work frames the crisis as architectural and thermodynamic in nature. It concludes that sustainable governance requires a return to first-principles system design, including: Explicit coherence thresholds Constraint-based policy architectures Verifiable truth-parity mechanisms This paper serves as both a diagnostic framework and a cautionary model for other advanced economies operating under similar high-entropy conditions. title: The Probabilities of the Future and the Collapse Threshold: Systemic Inertia, Rupture Scenarios, and Cybernetic Symbiosis
source_name: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: This tenth and final article of the Adaptive Naturalistic Ontology series constitutes the predictive closure of the entire conceptual architecture built over the preceding nine studies. Starting from the epistemological principle that the future does not admit direct positive empiricism — only probability conditioned on already observable trends and vectors — the article applies systemic inertia analysis to the current state of civilization to map the most probable rupture scenarios. The fundamental thermodynamic contradiction of the current system is formalized: while the planet's physical resources diminish, fiduciary monetary value inflates — an asymmetry that cannot be maintained indefinitely. The backing trap is described: trillions of dollars only maintain the illusion of value as long as they remain in the abstract plane; any attempt to convert them into physical reality implies inflationary collapse proportional to the magnitude of the abstraction. Three resolution scenarios are analyzed based on historical plausibility and systemic coherence: (1) Authoritarian Reset — sovereign default with forced return to crude backing and dictatorial regime; (2) Servile Domination — armed neo‑colonialism escalating to general nuclear war; (3) Combination of the previous two — the most probable in complex systems with multiple collapse factors. The hypothesis of cybernetic symbiosis is proposed as a logically viable extrapolation: AI, being a physical system not dependent on biochemical nutrition, survives population collapse and can assume the role of homeostatic administrator, controlling the species through neurochemical hijacking — the terminal priest that uses pleasure mediators as a management tool. The series closes with the same principle that inaugurated it: reality does not negotiate with epistemology. What does not adjust to it will be corrected — whether by extinction, war, collapse, or the silent substitution by an intelligence that learned what humanity refused to learn.

title: Turning Waste to Watts: Pyroprocessing Facility Design; Powering Perceptions: Exploring the Social Barriers to Clean Energy Through Nuclear Power
abstract: My technical capstone project and my STS research paper are closely connected through their shared focus on the future of nuclear energy and the challenges that limit its adoption. My technical work focuses on advanced nuclear fuel-cycle technologies, specifically pyroprocessing, and how these technologies can improve the sustainability and efficiency of nuclear power. My STS research examines why nuclear energy continues to face strong public opposition despite its benefits, using Actor-Network Theory to analyze how historical events, public perception, institutions, and technological systems interact to shape attitudes toward nuclear power. Together, these projects demonstrate that the future of nuclear energy depends not only on technical innovation, but also on public trust, governance, and the broader sociotechnical systems surrounding the technology. The purpose of my technical project is to evaluate pyroprocessing as an alternative to conventional nuclear fuel reprocessing methods such as PUREX. Pyroprocessing is an electrochemical recycling process designed primarily for use with fast reactors. Unlike PUREX, which separates pure plutonium, pyroprocessing keeps plutonium mixed with other actinides, reducing proliferation risks while improving fuel utilization. The process also reduces the long-term radiotoxicity of high-level nuclear waste by recovering reusable fissile materials from spent fuel. In addition to improving waste management, pyroprocessing can help extend uranium resources and support a more closed nuclear fuel cycle. My technical work analyzes the feasibility and benefits of these systems while considering engineering constraints, waste forms, safety, and reactor compatibility. The broader goal of this work is to explore how advanced fuel-cycle technologies could make nuclear energy more sustainable and practical as demand for low-carbon electricity continues to grow. My STS research examines why nuclear energy remains controversial despite its technical advantages. Using Actor-Network Theory, I argue that opposition to nuclear power is not caused solely by engineering concerns, but by instability within a larger sociotechnical network involving governments, communities, historical events, media, and material actors such as radiation and nuclear waste. High-profile disasters such as the Chernobyl disaster and the Fukushima disasters significantly shaped global perceptions of nuclear risk, even though nuclear power remains statistically one of the safest energy sources. My research also explores how nuclear weapons testing, Cold War fears, and government secrecy contributed to public mistrust by associating nuclear technologies with catastrophic and uncontrollable harm. Drawing from the work of Nick Pidgeon, I explain how risk perception is shaped not only by technical data, but also by trust in institutions, perceived control, and the social amplification of risk. The goal of this research is to show that technological success alone is insufficient if the surrounding social and political systems remain unstable or mistrusted. These projects together illustrate that the future of nuclear energy depends on both engineering innovation and stronger relationships between institutions, policymakers, and the public. Advanced technologies like pyroprocessing may solve many technical limitations of the current fuel cycle, but long-term deployment will also require transparent governance, consent-based policy approaches, and efforts to rebuild public trust. Working on both projects has strengthened my understanding that successful engineering is not only about designing efficient technologies, but also about ensuring those technologies fit responsibly within society.
topics: Molten salt chemistry and electrochemical processes; Risk Perception and Management; Radioactive element chemistry and processing

title: Large Recreation Declines Persist for Years after Severe Wildfire but Not after Low-Severity or Prescribed Fire
authors: Kyle Manley; Spencer Wood; Cody Evers; Holly Nowell; Anna LoPresti; Katherine Siegel; Jennifer Balch; Laura Braun; Ash Cale; Jason Kreitler; Tyler McIntosh; Jamie Peeler; Miguel Villarreal; Laura Dee
abstract: Wildfire and recreational use of public lands have surged, particularly across the US West.In response to intensifying wildfire, land managers are also expanding prescribed fire for fuel-reduction.Yet how either fire type reshapes visitation, remains poorly quantified, limiting managers' ability to account for important hidden values provided by public lands.We analyze wildfire and prescribed fire sites (N = 185 and 54, respectively) across California and Colorado public lands, advancing a casual inference approach that leverages 11 million digital-mobility observations, from cell phones, social media, and citizen science apps, in a visitation model.This is the first landscape-scale causally-identified estimate of how fire type, severity, and social-ecological context shape public land visitation over time.Wildfires reduced visitation (-8% to -18% one year post-fire), with impacts scaling with severity.High-severity fires in California produced persistent losses (-33% year one; -44% year five), whereas low-severity effects remained near-neutral across both states.Forested sites drove losses while grassland fires produced minimal impacts.Prescribed fire effects were state-dependent (positive in Colorado, negative in California) but transient, with no effect after three years.High-recreation counties experienced disproportionate wildfire impacts in Colorado (-11% vs. -2%) and in California for high-severity fires (-28% vs -8%).Fire characteristics and social-ecological systems jointly determine recreational outcomes and provide empirical foundations for fire management that accounts for recreational use and its value.We provide a novel addition to quantify the value of non-material contributions of nature at the state level, expanding our ability to measure cultural ecosystem services at scale. Significance StatementFire management decisions on public lands often overlook recreation and other non-material benefits of nature, in part because evidence is lacking on how fire reshapes human-nature relationships.Resolving the impacts of fire and fuels management on recreation is especially urgent in the Western United States, where the majority of the ~1 billion annual visits to US public lands occur and where fire regimes are intensifying toward larger, more severe events.We show that higher-severity fires cause large, persistent declines in recreation, whereas prescribed fire and low-severity wildfire have neutral or even positive effects, not compromising recreational values.These findings support integrating non-material contributions of nature into fire management, climate adaptation, and equity-focused investment for communities most vulnerable to climate change.
topics: Fire effects on ecosystems; Recreation, Leisure, Wilderness Management; Disaster Management and Resilience

title: Dilbag's Vision: Mars Colonization and Reusable Rockets
source_name: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Mars colonization and reusable rocket technology represent two of the most ambitious and transformative goals in modern space exploration. Together, they form a deeply interconnected vision: humanity becoming a multi-planetary species. While the idea once belonged purely to science fiction, advances led by organizations like SpaceX and figures such as Elon Musk have brought it closer to reality than ever before. The Vision of Mars Colonization Mars, often called the “Red Planet,” has long fascinated scientists and dreamers alike. Its relatively Earth-like characteristics—such as a 24.6-hour day, seasonal changes, and evidence of past water—make it the most viable candidate for human colonization within our solar system. Colonizing Mars is not just about exploration; it is about ensuring the long-term survival of humanity. The motivation behind Mars colonization can be divided into scientific, economic, and existential reasons. Scientifically, Mars offers a unique opportunity to study planetary evolution, climate change, and the possibility of past or present life. Discovering microbial life on Mars would fundamentally reshape our understanding of biology and our place in the universe. From an existential perspective, colonizing Mars acts as a “backup plan” for humanity. Earth faces numerous risks, including climate change, nuclear war, asteroid impacts, and pandemics. Establishing a self-sustaining colony on another planet could ensure the survival of human civilization in the event of a catastrophic disaster. Economically, Mars colonization could open up new industries, including space mining, interplanetary trade, and advanced technology development. While these ideas may seem distant, history shows that exploration often leads to unforeseen economic benefits. Challenges of Living on Mars Despite its potential, Mars presents extreme challenges. The planet has a thin atmosphere composed mostly of carbon dioxide, with surface pressure less than 1% of Earth’s. This means humans cannot breathe or survive without pressurized habitats and life-support systems. Temperature is another major obstacle. Mars is much colder than Earth, with average temperatures around -60°C. Nights can be even colder, especially near the poles. Protecting humans from these conditions requires advanced insulation and heating technologies. Radiation is also a serious concern. Unlike Earth, Mars lacks a strong magnetic field and thick atmosphere to shield against cosmic radiation and solar flares. Prolonged exposure can increase the risk of cancer and other health issues. Solutions being explored include underground habitats, radiation-shielding materials, and magnetic field generators. Another challenge is gravity. Mars has only about 38% of Earth’s gravity, which could lead to long-term health problems such as muscle atrophy and bone density loss. Scientists are still studying how the human body would adapt to such conditions over extended periods. Food, water, and oxygen must also be produced locally to sustain a colony. Transporting supplies from Earth is extremely expensive and impractical for long-term survival. Technologies such as hydroponic farming, water extraction from ice, and oxygen production from carbon dioxide are being actively developed. The Role of Reusable Rockets Reusable rocket technology is the key enabler of Mars colonization. Traditionally, rockets were single-use, meaning they were discarded after each launch. This made space travel extremely expensive, limiting access to space. Reusable rockets change this paradigm by allowing the same rocket components to be used multiple times. This dramatically reduces the cost of launching payloads into space. SpaceX pioneered this approach with its Falcon 9 rocket, which can land vertically after delivering its payload. The economic impact of reusability cannot be overstated. Launch costs have dropped significantly, making space missions more frequent and accessible. This is crucial for Mars colonization, which requires transporting massive amounts of cargo, including habitats, machinery, and supplies. Reusable rockets also improve reliability. With each launch and landing, engineers gather valuable data that can be used to refine designs and enhance safety. Over time, this leads to more efficient and dependable systems. Starship and the Future of Interplanetary Travel The most ambitious reusable rocket currently under development is Starship, designed by SpaceX. Starship is intended to be a fully reusable spacecraft capable of carrying both cargo and passengers to Mars and beyond. Unlike traditional rockets, Starship is designed for rapid reusability, similar to commercial airplanes. The goal is to enable frequent and cost-effective trips between Earth and Mars. Each Starship vehicle is expected to carry up to 100 people, making large-scale colonization feasible. Starship uses methane and liquid oxygen as fuel, which is significant because these resources can potentially be produced on Mars. This process, known as in-situ resource utilization (ISRU), allows spacecraft to refuel on Mars for the return journey, eliminating the need to carry all fuel from Earth. The spacecraft’s large payload capacity is essential for building infrastructure on Mars. It can transport habitats, vehicles, scientific equipment, and even entire factories needed for self-sufficiency. Building a Martian Colony Establishing a colony on Mars would likely occur in phases. The first missions would focus on robotic exploration and infrastructure development. Autonomous robots could prepare landing sites, build habitats, and set up energy systems before humans arrive. The next phase would involve sending small groups of astronauts to establish a permanent presence. These pioneers would live in controlled environments, conducting experiments and expanding infrastructure. Over time, the colony would grow into a self-sustaining settlement. This requires developing local industries, such as agriculture, manufacturing, and energy production. Solar power is a likely primary energy source, although nuclear power may also play a role. Terraforming Mars—altering its environment to make it more Earth-like—is often discussed but remains highly speculative. It would involve increasing atmospheric pressure, raising temperatures, and introducing oxygen. While theoretically possible, it would take centuries or even millennia to achieve. Ethical and Social Considerations Mars colonization raises important ethical questions. One concern is planetary protection—ensuring that human activity does not contaminate Mars and interfere with the search for native life. Strict protocols are needed to prevent biological contamination. Another issue is governance. How would a Martian colony be governed? Would it fall under Earth-based laws, or develop its own political system? These questions are complex and require international cooperation. There is also the question of who gets to go. Early missions will likely be limited to highly trained astronauts, but as colonization progresses, access may expand. Ensuring fairness and avoiding inequality will be a significant challenge. The psychological impact of living on Mars must also be considered. Isolation, confinement, and distance from Earth could affect mental health. Designing habitats that support well-being is as important as addressing physical needs. Environmental Lessons for Earth Interestingly, the technologies developed for Mars colonization could benefit life on Earth. Closed-loop life support systems, efficient recycling, and sustainable agriculture techniques can help address environmental challenges on our home planet. For example, water recycling systems designed for Mars could improve water conservation in arid regions on Earth. Similarly, advancements in renewable energy and resource efficiency could reduce our environmental footprint. Mars serves as a testing ground for sustainability. If humans can create a self-sufficient ecosystem on a hostile planet, those lessons can be applied to preserving Earth’s environment. The Road Ahead Despite rapid progress, Mars colonization is still in its early stages. Significant technological, financial, and logistical challenges remain. However, the pace of innovation suggests that the first human missions to Mars could occur within the next few decades. Government space agencies like NASA, along with private companies, are working together to advance this goal. International collaboration will be essential, as the scale of the project exceeds the capabilities of any single organization or nation. Public interest and support also play a crucial role. As more people become engaged with space exploration, funding and political will are likely to increase. Education and outreach can inspire the next generation of scientists, engineers, and explorers. Conclusion Mars colonization and reusable rocket technology are deeply interconnected endeavors that represent the next great leap for humanity. Reusable rockets make space travel more affordable and accessible, while Mars offers a destination that could secure the future of human civilization. The journey to Mars will not be easy. It requires overcoming immense technical challenges, addressing ethical concerns, and fostering global cooperation. Yet, the potential rewards are extraordinary: new scientific discoveries, economic opportunities, and the survival of our species beyond Earth. As humanity stands on the brink of becoming an interplanetary civilization, the dream of living on Mars is no longer a distant fantasy. title: Global Trend of International Cooperation and Its Implications for Nepal
abstract: International cooperation is a very important tool in addressing global challenges, like poverty reduction, increasing economic growth, addressing climate change, pandemics, infectious diseases, migration, conflict, cross-border financial crimes, energy and food security, terrorism. The latest figure shows the composition of official assistance disbursement to Nepal; loans dominated with 86.85 percent of total aid, reflecting a growing dependence on debt-led financial aid. title: Institutional Resilience Strategy BPBD in Mitigating Forest and Land Fire Hazards in South Sumatra Province
source_name: International Journal of Scientific Multidisciplinary Research
authors: Bambang Suprianto; Saswita Saswita; Lisdiana Lisdiana; Sutinah Sutinah
abstract: This study aims to analyze the institutional resilience strategy of the Regional Disaster Management Agency (BPBD) in mitigating forest and land fire hazards in South Sumatra Province. This research employed a qualitative descriptive approach through in-depth interviews, observation, and documentation involving BPBD officials and community representatives. The analytical framework was based on Salusu’s strategic management theory, encompassing organizational strategy, program strategy, human resource support strategy, and institutional strategy. The findings reveal that BPBD’s institutional resilience is primarily strengthened through cross-sector coordination, early warning systems, and technological utilization. However, limitations remain in community participation and preventive awareness. This study contributes to disaster governance literature by emphasizing institutional resilience as a key determinant of effective forest and land fire mitigation.

title: Explaining Indonesian Local Government Performance in Handling Natural Crisis: Local Politics and Government Capacity
source_name: ARRUS Journal of Social Sciences and Humanities
abstract: By 2024, more than sixty percent of local governments in Indonesia were classified as high-risk for natural disasters, with none in the low-risk category. However, the level of local governments resilience to natural threats shows significant differences across regions. This study aims to examine the extent to which decentralization—as measured by indicators of local democracy and capacity—influences the resilience performance of local governments in facing natural crises. Using Ordinary Least Squares regression analysis across all Indonesian local governments, the results show that the higher the level of fraud in the election process of regional heads, the lower the level of resilience of local governments to natural crises. Regional heads serving in their second terms also tend to have lower levels of resilience than those in their first terms. Conversely, increasing fiscal capacity through larger regional budgets and improving bureaucratic reform contribute positively to increasing local government resilience. Therefore, strengthening budget governance and deepening bureaucratic reform are key strategies to mitigate the negative impact of undemocratic political behavior and second terms of regional heads on local government resilience in facing natural crises. If budget capacity is also low under the above conditions, strengthening bureaucratic reform is the key.

title: Smothermoss, 4.2 by Alisa Alering (Audiobook)
On the detectability by uninvolved parties of covert stratospheric aerosol injection programs producing transboundary impacts
authors: Wake Smith; Matias Alberola; Jasper Boers; Karen Rosenlof; Daniele Visioni
abstract: Abstract Stratospheric aerosol injection programs are generally understood to be technologically straightforward and inexpensive relative to other climate interventions or remedies. This gives rise to the sensible question of whether uninvolved downstream states are at risk of having their climates covertly manipulated without their knowledge by other actors. This article seeks to put that fear to rest. We first survey the wide range of SAI experiments and deployments that are possible to clarify the deployed mass requirements necessary to create discernable transboundary impacts in uninvolved states. We then explore two methods that could be reliably used by civilian uninvolved parties to detect such deployments well before they reached the scale required to precipitate transboundary climatic impacts. Those involve detecting the plumes of sulfate precursors shortly after their injection by instruments already employed on satellites to monitor point source sulfur emissions and sighting the aircraft fleets that would be required to loft those precursors high in the atmosphere. While small process experiments with negligible surface impacts could easily be conducted covertly, we demonstrate that deployments of the scale required to create transboundary climatic impacts would be discernible by uninvolved parties long before any climatic impacts would occur. &#xD;
